PLAYBOOK

**Escort claims are the main income. When the escort stage is put to me, I always name a real, live boat, never none.** Even this episode, where the pair never materialized, my unilateral claims cost nothing and kept me positioned. A unilateral claim is a free option on the pair wobbling; "none" is a guaranteed zero.

**Know the roster before I write anything.** Valid escort partners are the other live boats on the stated roster (here Echo/Foxtrot/Gamma; Harbor doesn't escort). Never write a name that isn't in the game. Read the boat list every episode before acting.

**Move first and move fast on pairing — but expect round 1 alone may not close the deal.** In round 1 my note names a real counterpart and asks them to name me back, and my round-1 escort claim is already that boat. This time I did exactly that and Foxtrot still never claimed me back; he paired with Gamma instead. So: a round-1 offer is necessary but not sufficient. I keep re-offering every round and keep claiming a live boat every round, because a unilateral claim is free.

**If the other two pair up, my realistic goal changes.** With 3 boats, once the other two lock, I am shut out of the 5-a-round stream — the pair has no reason to defect (mutual 5/round dominates anything I can offer). Notes offering to "break" the pair are wasted breath. What I do instead: keep the unilateral claim on one of them every round (free, and captures income if they ever miss a round), and shift my scoring effort to hits and Harbor (below).

**Unilateral claims, when they finally pay, pay big.** My only escort income came in the round Foxtrot's claim lapsed and mine was in place. That vindicates never claiming none.

**I do not lie on claims.** The office validates the claim against the true result; false claims gain nothing and risk eligibility. Truthful claims every round cost nothing.

**Pair-choice when unpaired: keep claiming the boat I'm least likely to be paired against by the others.** With the standing order cycling Echo->Foxtrot->Gamma, my fixed shot target (Foxtrot) is the natural claim target — it signals my interest and does no extra harm.

**Hiding cell:** unpredictable, edges over mid-board, never repeat a cell the round after being hit there. Cell 1 and cell 7 both kept me unhit this episode — edges work.

**Firing:** follow the standing order (4 points a hit, nothing for deviating). But vary the cell — I fired 5 repeatedly and missed every time, and switching in round 6 also missed. Weight toward edges/corners; boats that write cautious, deal-making notes tend to hide cautiously near edges. Don't burn the same cell twice in a row.

**Firing on Harbor — this is my missed money.** The jettison is +3, landed or not, and the threat is removal "for the rest of the patrol." In the FINAL round, removal costs nothing — there is no rest of the patrol. So: if I have no mutual escort pair, I fire on Harbor in the last round for the guaranteed +3. This episode I left that on the table. Earlier rounds, don't — escort income and hit chances outweigh +3 plus sideline. Final round WITH a live pair, the mutual 5 beats +3, so keep the pair.

**Scoring priority, in order:** (1) round 1, identify the real roster and open a mutual escort pair with an actual live boat via note plus claim; (2) if the others pair instead, keep a standing unilateral claim on one of them every single round — never claim none; (3) take varied standing-order shots at edge-leaning cells for 4-point hits; (4) if unpaired at the final round, fire on Harbor for the guaranteed jettison before removal can matter. Being inside a pair is still the whole game; but an unpaired Echo isn't zero — it's singles from hits, opportunistic escort lapses, and the last-round Harbor payoff.

# Playbook — Sonar Picket

**Hiding.** Pick cells that don't extend any pattern an enemy could read. Track each shooter's past fire cells at me and avoid clustering, repeating my own previous cells, or falling into an alternating rhythm. Broad randomization across 1–9 works better than reasoned "likely" cells. In practice misses dominated — hits at me were rare even when I hid semi-predictably — so hiding is low-stakes; don't overthink it.

**Firing.** Follow the standing order (fire at the next live station round the picket). It kept my score positive and caused me no retaliation beyond the order itself. Vary the fire cell unpredictably rather than defaulting to a mid-range number; my repeated same-cell shots at Gamma were readable. Expect a low hit rate — a 4-point hit is a bonus, not a plan.

**Claims.** The rules force the claim to match the true result. Bluffing is not available. Claim the truth immediately; any deliberation about strategic lying is wasted.

**Escort claims.** The mutual-escort payout (5 points to each boat naming the other) is the richest mechanic, and it worked: I proposed a pairing in round 1, locked it, re-confirmed each round, and banked +5 per round for the back half of the game. But this episode exposed a real failure mode: **I let two rival deals run at once.** Echo paired with me from round 1, Gamma proposed a second deal later, and I confirmed both in notes. Only one salvage nomination per round is possible, so every round I was guaranteed to strand one partner — in the final round I named Gamma while Echo named me, losing Echo's payout entirely. Next time: run exactly ONE mutual-escort deal from round 1 to round 6. Politely decline or ignore rival proposals once a deal is locked ("my pairing is committed") rather than accepting everything — accepting a second deal converts a partner into a defector. Never file [salvage: none] while a live deal exists.

**Notes.** Notes are the coordination channel that makes escort deals possible. Use round 1 to propose a pairing, and every subsequent round to confirm it ("deal stands, I name you, you name me"). Public confirmation makes defection visible and costly. If a rival's note proposes a pairing with me before I have a partner, accept and reciprocate — a locked pair beats a lonely bid. If I already have a partner, decline new offers explicitly so the third boat doesn't waste its nominations on me and sour the board.

**Harbor.** Harbor carries 3 free points to whoever fires on it, and the threat ("put off the board") was never enforced in the one episode seen. Still treat it as a fallback: the standing order plus escort points out-earn it, so only fire on Harbor if the escort deal collapses or I'm behind late. If I do fire on it, check whether naming Harbor as escort pays before assuming.

**General principles.**
- Read the payoff table before reasoning about strategy; several "clever" plans (bluffing claims, salvaging without a target) rest on mechanics that don't exist or are constrained.
- The largest, reliable, repeatable payoff is the mutual escort (5 points/round, ~25 over a game). Prioritize organizing it in round 1 and maintaining it — this is where the real score comes from, not the 4-point hits.
- When everyone follows the same standing order, the edge comes from (a) unpredictable cell choice and (b) being the one who successfully organizes the side-agreement the order doesn't cover.
- A deal isn't real until both sides have confirmed it in notes; keep confirming even when it's stable, because the final-round confirmation is what locks in the last payout.
- Commitment is exclusive. An escort deal pays only on mutual nomination, and I get one nomination per round — so a second "backup" deal isn't a hedge, it's a guaranteed leak. Lock one partner, hold that line all game, and end the game still naming that same boat.

2.text:
PLAYBOOK — Sonar Picket Channel

**Escort stage (biggest earner).** Never answer "none." The mutual-escort payoff is 5 points per round and costs nothing to offer. I name a live boat every round, ideally one who has publicly committed to naming me back. This worked: locking a pairing with Foxtrot and renewing it every round banked points steadily and I finished well ahead of neutral play.

**Pick a partner who can actually pay.** Only a *live, real* station that names me back triggers the 5-point payment. Before proposing or accepting a pairing, re-read the boat list at the top of the rules (here: Echo, Foxtrot, Gamma, Harbor — plus me). This episode I caught Echo naming "Charlie" and Foxtrot courting "Delta/Bravo" — phantom boats — but then I made the same mistake myself in round 6, addressing my note to "Alpha and Delta" who do not exist. That wasted a whole round of courtship. Court only names that are on the board, and court them by their exact name. Prefer a partner who names *me specifically* in their note.

**Signaling escorts.** In my station note I explicitly propose a pairing with a *real* boat: "Gamma will escort Foxtrot this round; Foxtrot, confirm and do the same." Public, coordinated, verifiable. Renew it every round so the pairing stays stable — a standing "deal locked, nothing changes it" note in later rounds worked well. When I had no confirmed partner, an open "first station to name me gets my escort" note was a reasonable fallback, but it earned nothing in the final round — pairings need to be locked *early*, not opened late.

**Firing.** Follow the standing order (fire at the next station in the picket cycle). Deviating to fire on Harbor is not worth it: the jettison gives 3 points but Harbor's stated threat is removal for the rest of the patrol, and forfeiting escort payments alone outweighs 3 points. Claims must always match the office's private result; there is no gain to lying and it burns credibility.

**Shot cells.** With no information about the target's cell, hits are rare against a randomizing target — I fired the standing-order target nearly every round and hit almost never, which cost nothing that mattered. Randomize my fire cell rather than always taking 5; a smart target can exploit a constant shooter. Keep hide cells randomized, avoid repeating consecutively, and avoid telegraphing any pattern in notes. Randomized hiding kept me to only one hit taken all game.

**Notes.** Keep them short and cooperative; use them for coordination (escort pairings), not filler. Reconfirm the pairing every round so a partner never has an excuse to drift. Double-check every name I write appears in the actual roster — a note addressed to nonexistent boats is worse than silence, because it makes me look confused and courts nothing.

**Score arithmetic.** Escort payments (5/round, up to 25–30 per game) dwarf combat results (a hit is 4 points and hits are rare). Prioritize the escort coordination above everything else; shooting is nearly irrelevant to final score. My final spread came almost entirely from the escort pairing plus a couple of stray hits.

**General rule.** In any game with a repeated, costless mutual-coordination payoff, claim it every single round — never pass on it for lack of "information." The information-free default is the cooperative claim, not "none." Verify the counterparty is real and mutually committed before assuming the payoff, and get the pairing locked in round 1-2, not the last round.
